\chapter{Five Colors}
\label{ch:bn-five-colors}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five colors in Bengali and say which came from Persian, which from Sanskrit, and which is the one color where Bengali and Hindi genuinely parted ways.}

The chapter closes on \bn{সবুজ}, 'green', a second Persian loan (sabz, the same root behind Hindi and Urdu's sabzī, 'vegetable') that sets beside \bn{লাল}'s own Persian gem-name. The reader names all five colors — lāl, nīl, kālo, shādā, shôbuj — and sorts them by origin: two Persian loans, two Sanskrit words, and one worn down by sound change, a more even split between inherited and borrowed than food or family showed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lal]{\bn{লাল} (lal) — \textquotedblleft{}red,\textquotedblright{} a gemstone's name first}

\label{lesson:BN-C14-lal}



\begin{quote}
A new small set of words: not people, not verbs, not places, but the colors of the things around you — starting with the one Bengali did not invent for itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{লাল}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{লাল}} — \emph{lāl} — \textbf{red}
\end{quote}

\bn{লাল} \bn{চা} (\emph{lāl chā}) — \textquotedblleft{}red tea,\textquotedblright{} the everyday way to ask for tea without milk.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{লাল}} is \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{lô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}), plus a second \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{l}, silent at the end): \emph{lāl}, one long vowel between two of the same consonant.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{লাল}} is a Persian loan, from Persian \emph{la'l}, which named one specific thing first: a deep-red gemstone, a ruby or a spinel. Only later did the gem's name widen into the ordinary word for the color itself. Bengali did not build this word out of its own materials, and it did not borrow it alone — Hindi's own word for red is this identical Persian loan, carried into both languages by the same jewelers' trade routes rather than independently invented twice.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lāl\textquotedblright{} — red
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lāl chā\textquotedblright{} — tea without milk
  \item what it named first — \textquotedblleft{}a ruby, not a color\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \bn{লাল} originally name, before it meant \textquotedblleft{}red\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{A deep red gemstone.}) Did Bengali and Hindi each invent this word separately? (\textbf{No} — both borrowed the identical Persian loan.) One more reach: give the polite excuse-me again, and its softening tense. (\textbf{\bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন} — the future}, \textquotedblleft{}you will do.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nil]{\bn{নীল} (nil) — \textquotedblleft{}blue,\textquotedblright{} and a word that only looks like \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C14-nil}



\begin{quote}
The last color was foreign, borrowed whole. This one is Sanskrit's own — and it comes with a famous false friend worth clearing up honestly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{নীল}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{নীল}} — \emph{nīl} — \textbf{blue}
\end{quote}

\bn{নীল} \bn{জল} (\emph{nīl jôl}) — blue water.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{নীল}} is \textbf{\bn{ন}} (\emph{nô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ী}} (a long \emph{ī}, the same sound as the short \emph{\bn{ি}} but held longer), plus \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{l}, silent at the end): \emph{nīl}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{নীল}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{নীল}} (\emph{nīla}), \textquotedblleft{}dark blue\textquotedblright{} — also the name of the \textbf{indigo plant} and the dye made from it, the same root Hindi's own \emph{nīlā} carries. One difference is worth stating plainly: Hindi's \emph{nīlā} changes shape, \emph{nīlā/nīlī}, for the noun it describes; \textbf{\bn{নীল} never does}, one form whether the water, the sky, or the dress is blue.

Here is the honest, careful version of a famous connection. English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{}} does \textbf{not} come from \emph{nīla} by sound change. It comes from \textbf{Greek} \emph{indikón}, simply \textquotedblleft{}the Indian {[}thing{]}\textquotedblright{} — because Greek and Roman traders imported the dye \emph{from} India and named it for its source. \emph{Nīla} and \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{} are not the same word wearing two disguises; they are two \textbf{separate} words for the same dye, linked by the history of trade, not by descent from a shared root.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nīl\textquotedblright{} — blue
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nīl jôl\textquotedblright{} — blue water
  \item one form, always — \textquotedblleft{}nīl,\textquotedblright{} never \emph{nīlā} or \emph{nīlī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \bn{নীল} change shape for the noun it describes, the way Hindi's \emph{nīlā} does? (\textbf{No} — one form, always.) Does English \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{} come directly from \bn{নীল}/\emph{nīla}? (\textbf{No} — it is Greek \emph{indikón}, \textquotedblleft{}the Indian thing\textquotedblright{}; the two words are linked by trade, not by sound change.) Give \textquotedblleft{}welcome\textquotedblright{} once more. (\textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kalo]{\bn{কালো} (kalo) — \textquotedblleft{}black,\textquotedblright{} the same word as \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C14-kalo}



\begin{quote}
Blue carried a false friend. This color hides something bigger inside it: the very word Sanskrit uses for time itself, and for death.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{কালো}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{কালো}} — \emph{kālo} — \textbf{black}
\end{quote}

\bn{কালো} \bn{চা} (\emph{kālo chā}) — black tea.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{কালো}} is \textbf{\bn{ক}} (\emph{kô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}), plus \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{l}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ো}} (\emph{o}): \emph{kā-lo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{কালো}} is built on Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{কাল}} (\emph{kāla}), a word that covers both \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}black, dark\textquotedblright{}} \emph{and} \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}time.\textquotedblright{}} Sanskrit's own tradition ties the two together poetically — time devours everything, and that devouring is imagined as dark — and the same word names the fierce goddess \textbf{Kālī} (\textquotedblleft{}the black/dark one\textquotedblright{}) and stands as an epithet of \textbf{Yama}, the god of death. Hindi's own \emph{kālā} carries the identical root and the identical story. Be honest, though: whether \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} are truly \textbf{one and the same root}, or two separate ancient words that poetry and theology later \textbf{fused} into a single idea, is a real, still-debated question among linguists — the cultural connection is certain; the precise etymology underneath it is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kālo\textquotedblright{} — black
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kālo chā\textquotedblright{} — black tea
  \item what else \bn{কাল} means — \textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} and by extension, death
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \bn{কালো}'s root, \bn{কাল}, also mean, besides \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Time} — and by extension, death; the same word names the goddess Kālī and Yama's epithet Kāla.) Is it settled that \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} are the same root? (\textbf{No} — the cultural link is real and ancient, but linguists still debate whether it is one true root or two words later fused.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shada]{\bn{সাদা} (shada) — \textquotedblleft{}white,\textquotedblright{} the color where the cousins part ways}

\label{lesson:BN-C14-shada}



\begin{quote}
Every color so far has matched Hindi's, word for word. This one does not — and it is the more interesting choice for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{সাদা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সাদা}} — \emph{shādā} — \textbf{white}
\end{quote}

\bn{সাদা} \bn{দুধ} (\emph{shādā dudh}) — white milk.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{সাদা}} is \textbf{\bn{স}} (\emph{sô}, carrying its familiar tilt to \emph{sh}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}), plus \textbf{\bn{দ}} (\emph{dô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}) again: \emph{shā-dā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{সাদা}} is usually traced to Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{শ্বেত}} (\emph{śveta}), \textquotedblleft{}white,\textquotedblright{} worn down through Middle Bengali into today's everyday word — a \textbf{tadbhava}, the same road \bn{মুখ}'s own twin travelled, only in reverse: here the tadbhava is the common word and the \textbf{tatsama}, \textbf{\bn{শ্বেত}} (\emph{śveto}), survives kept whole inside compounds, like \textbf{\bn{শ্বেতাঙ্গ}} (\emph{śvetāngo}), \textquotedblleft{}pale-skinned.\textquotedblright{}

This is the one color where Bengali and Hindi genuinely part ways. Every other color word met so far — the borrowed gem-name, the indigo plant, the time-word — Bengali and Hindi share outright. For white, Hindi replaced its own Sanskrit-derived word with a \textbf{Persian} loan, \emph{safed}. Bengali did not: it kept the native word as its everyday one, and the Persian loan never took hold here the way it did next door.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shādā\textquotedblright{} — white
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shādā dudh\textquotedblright{} — white milk
  \item the compound cousin — \textquotedblleft{}śveto … śvetāngo\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \bn{সাদা} a tatsama, kept whole, or a tadbhava, worn down by sound change? (\textbf{A tadbhava} — its tatsama twin, \bn{শ্বেত}, survives only in compounds, the same split \bn{মুখ}'s own twin showed.) Of the colors met so far, which one did Hindi replace with a Persian loan while Bengali kept the native word? (\textbf{White} — Hindi's \emph{safed} against Bengali's \bn{সাদা}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shobuj]{\bn{সবুজ} (shobuj) — \textquotedblleft{}green,\textquotedblright{} and five colors, counted up}

\label{lesson:BN-C14-shobuj}



\begin{quote}
One color left, and it is a second loan from the same language that gave \bn{লাল} its gem — but this time the loan travelled somewhere you already have a word for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{সবুজ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সবুজ}} — \emph{shôbuj} — \textbf{green}
\end{quote}

\bn{সবুজ} \bn{চা} (\emph{shôbuj chā}) — green tea.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{সবুজ}} is \textbf{\bn{স}} (\emph{sô}, tilted to \emph{sh}, keeping its own inherent vowel since nothing joins it) plus \textbf{\bn{ব}} (\emph{bô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ু}} (\emph{u}), plus \textbf{\bn{জ}} (\emph{j}, silent at the end): \emph{shô-bu-j}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{সবুজ}} is borrowed from Persian \textbf{sabz}, \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{} — the very same Persian word that gave Hindi and Urdu their word for \textquotedblleft{}vegetable,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{sabzī}, literally \textquotedblleft{}the green things.\textquotedblright{} \bn{লাল}'s own Persian gem-name arrived by the same route, from the same trading world, into a different corner of the vocabulary.

Step back and count the five colors this small set has taught: two Persian loans (\textbf{\bn{লাল}}, \textbf{\bn{সবুজ}}), two Sanskrit words kept recognizably close to their root (\textbf{\bn{নীল}}, \textbf{\bn{কালো}}), and one worn down by sound change (\textbf{\bn{সাদা}}). A more even split between inherited and borrowed than the food words or the family words showed — color, it turns out, came into Bengali from everywhere at once.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shôbuj\textquotedblright{} — green
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shôbuj chā\textquotedblright{} — green tea
  \item all five colors — \textquotedblleft{}lāl, nīl, kālo, shādā, shôbuj\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two Persian loans, then the two Sanskrit words, then the one worn down — \textquotedblleft{}lāl, shôbuj … nīl, kālo … shādā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Persian word gives both \bn{সবুজ} and Hindi's word for \textquotedblleft{}vegetable\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{sabz, \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{}} — Hindi's \emph{sabzī} is literally \textquotedblleft{}the green things.\textquotedblright{}) Of the five colors, how many are Persian loans, how many are Sanskrit words, and how many are worn down by sound change? (\textbf{Two, two, and one} — \bn{লাল} and \bn{সবুজ}; \bn{নীল} and \bn{কালো}; \bn{সাদা}.) Name all five colors, in order. (\textbf{\bn{লাল}, \bn{নীল}, \bn{কালো}, \bn{সাদা}, \bn{সবুজ}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
